narrative:
Short impact summary

Teachers’ Competencies has shown substantial scholarly uptake since its 2010 publication, with 264 citations in OpenAlex and a field- and year-normalized standing in the top 10% of cited works. Its influence is concentrated in education research, but the citation record also shows reach across psychology, linguistics, sociology, and philosophy.

Full narrative

Teachers’ Competencies has developed into a clearly influential scholarly article. The OpenAlex record shows 264 citations, placing it in the top 10% of cited works for its field and publication year. That level of uptake is reinforced by a downstream reuse graph of the same size, indicating that the article has been taken up broadly across later scholarship rather than remaining a narrowly referenced source.

The citing literature is rooted overwhelmingly in education, with most reuse appearing in journal articles, alongside conference papers, book chapters, books, dissertations, preprints, reviews, and related scholarly formats. The venues that cite it most often include International Journal of Learning Teaching and Educational Research, Procedia - Social and Behavioral Sciences, SAGE Open, International Journal of Instruction, and Sustainability, suggesting that the article has become part of an active conversation about teacher development, instructional practice, and competency frameworks.

The topical profile of the citing work points to durable relevance in teacher education and leadership, curriculum and learning methods, educational communication, school leadership, and technology-enhanced education. Citations are geographically distributed, with especially strong representation from Indonesia, followed by Turkey, the Philippines, China, Malaysia, the United States, Iran, and Russia. This pattern indicates that the article has been useful across multiple educational contexts, not only within a single regional or institutional network.

More recent citations show that the work continues to inform current discussions of teacher competence, including professional competence, measurement of teacher performance, and systematic reviews of competency-related constructs. Scite records 4 supporting citation statements and a larger body of mentioning citations, which is consistent with a paper that is repeatedly used as a conceptual reference point. At the same time, the public-discourse record is quiet in the available sources, so the strongest evidence of impact remains scholarly rather than broader online attention.
